title: は and が: the deeper secrets
summary: は marks old, known information and throws the weight onto what follows; が marks the new information, often the answer to a question.

blocks.text: Every Japanese sentence has a **topic** and a **subject**. When you see neither, both are **zero**: 日本人です is really (zero は)(zero が)日本人です. The choice between **は** and **が** only exists when the topic and the subject are the same thing, and then you are not creating either one. You are **stressing** which role the word plays, and that changes what the sentence implies.

**は** can only mark **old information**: something the listener already knows or will easily accept. Old information is the unimportant part of a sentence, so **は** pushes the weight onto whatever comes after it. **が** can mark new information, and when it does, the new thing is the word itself.

blocks.en: (I) bought a book. (neutral: nothing is stressed)
As for me, I bought a book. (answers "What did you do?")
I am the one who bought the book. (answers "Who bought it?")

blocks.text: Imagine two friends staring at an empty gap on a shelf. They know the book is gone, so the book is old information. The new information is **who** took it, so you say 私**が**買った.
Because of this, **が** tends to point at particular things and **は** at general ones. These are tendencies, not laws: the listener decides from what sounds natural.

blocks.en: Flowers are beautiful. (flowers in general are the topic)

blocks.text: は for contrast and for emphasis

The plain way to report weather is 雨**が**降っている. Say 雨**は**降っている and you imply a contrast: rain, at least, is falling (perhaps you expected snow). Used as a sub-topic, **は** also throws emphasis forward onto the engine, as in 休み**は**ない: "as for rest, there is none."

blocks.en: Rain is falling (but something else you expected is not).

items: A sentence always has a topic and a subject, visible or zero.
**は** marks old information and pushes the weight forward; it cannot introduce something new.
**が** can mark new information: the word itself is the answer.
**が** leans toward the particular, **は** toward the general. Learn what sounds natural by immersion.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap (the answer is new information)
questions.prompt: 「誰がケーキを食べましたか。」「弟＿＿食べました。」
questions.note: The answer to "who" is new information, so が.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap (the person is already known)
questions.prompt: 「あの人は誰ですか。」「あの人＿＿田中さんです。」
questions.en: "Who is that person?" "That person is Mr. Tanaka."
questions.note: The person is old information, so は.

questions.instruction: Which sentence answers "Who came?"
questions.note: が puts the new information on the word itself.

questions.instruction: Which sentence is more likely to state a general truth about cats?
questions.note: は tends toward the general, が toward the particular.

questions.instruction: What does は add here?
options: A contrast with something else (maybe the food was not touched)
questions.en: (I) did drink the beer (but maybe not something else).
questions.note: は can imply a contrast.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap (a neutral report)
questions.prompt: 窓の外を見て！雪＿＿降っている。
questions.note: A plain weather report uses が; は would hint at a contrast.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap (a sub-topic that stresses the engine)
questions.note: は as a sub-topic throws emphasis onto ない.

questions.instruction: Which particle can mark new information?
questions.note: は can only mark old information.

questions.instruction: A friend asks, "What did you do yesterday?" Which answer fits best?
questions.note: The question is about what you did; 私は is old information.

questions.instruction: Which line starts a story naturally: "Long ago an old man lived (there)"?
options: むかしむかし、おじいさんは住んでいました。
むかしむかし、おじいさんが住んでいました。
questions.note: The old man is new to the listener, so が.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that holds the old information
questions.note: The book is already known; 私が is the new part.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that carries the new information
questions.note: This dish is already known; the new thing is who made it.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: As for me, I drink coffee every morning.
questions.en: As for me, I drink coffee every morning.
questions.note: は marks the old information first.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: Mr. Tanaka is the one who phoned me.
questions.en: Mr. Tanaka is the one who phoned me.
questions.note: が puts the weight on 田中さん as the new information.

questions.instruction: True or false? In the lesson's basic rule, は marks old information, something the listener already knows.
questions.note: Old information is the unimportant part, so は pushes weight forward.

questions.instruction: A asks whether rain and snow fell. What does B's answer imply?
options: Rain, at least, fell; something else maybe did not
questions.en: It did rain (but maybe not snow).
questions.note: は adds contrast with the other thing.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap (introducing something new)
questions.prompt: あそこに大きい木＿＿ある。
questions.en: There is a big tree over there.
questions.note: The tree is new to the listener, so が.

questions.instruction: Why is 先生は来た a poor answer to "Who came?"
options: は marks old information, but the answer is new information
来た is a present tense
questions.note: The word that answers "who" is new information, so it takes が.

questions.instruction: When the topic and the subject are the same word, what does choosing は or が do?
options: Stresses which role the word plays
questions.note: You are not creating either one; you are stressing one.

questions.instruction: When a sentence like 学生です shows neither a topic nor a subject, what are they?
questions.note: Every sentence has both; when invisible they are zeros.

questions.instruction: Which sentence shows neither a topic nor a subject?
questions.note: Both are left as zeros: a neutral statement.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap (you see it for the first time)
questions.note: Something newly noticed takes が.
